name: Carla Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Riverside Homes, a housing association that rents flats to people on lower incomes. I open the post at half eight, book repair visits for tenants, file tenancy papers and type up the minutes from the Tuesday team meeting. I like it when a tenant rings back to say the plumber actually turned up. What wears me out is the new booking system, which keeps suggesting times I didn't pick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are you finding it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just over a year. I'm still slower than Denise (the senior admin), and she corrects my filing more than I'd like. The pay is good for this kind of job because it's a union workplace, and I've got a decent cushion from my gran, so I'm not scared of rent. I just like doing things my own way, with my paper diary next to the keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at Riverside Homes got excited about the AI booking tool, and it can't tell a burst pipe from a dripping tap. I'd say it online too, probably with a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not completely. Even a small tool takes the boring bits, and the boring bits are most of what a junior like me does. If the system books the repairs itself, my manager might ask what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and keep my paper diary. I'd go to the union branch meeting I keep skipping, because they're talking about rules for new software. And I'd keep my savings where they are, in the boring account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little bit like someone has moved my desk two inches to the left and won't say why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you miss least, and which would hurt to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd happily lose the meeting minutes, they're dull. Booking repairs is different, because I talk to the tenants and I know Mrs Okafor on the third floor can't do mornings. A machine doesn't know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not scared of rent. What does keep you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to be fair. Tomas (my partner) drives buses and we split everything, and I've got about eleven months saved. What bugs me is being made to feel stupid by software I never asked for.

say: The AI hype was **overblown**, and the booking tool still can't tell a burst pipe from a drip.
Tenants need a **person** who knows them, not a system that guesses.
think: Even small tools eat the **boring tasks**, and those are most of a junior's day.
If repairs book themselves, my **manager** may wonder what I'm for.
do: Keep using my **paper diary** and doing bookings by phone with tenants.
Go to the **union branch** meeting about rules for new office software.
Leave my **savings** untouched in the ordinary account.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small itch of **irritation** at software I didn't choose.
S0.quote: Even a small tool takes the boring bits, and the boring bits are most of what a junior like me does.
fieldNote: Her **cushion** from her gran and a partner's wage mean money isn't the worry.
The real sore spot is **pride**: being made to feel slow by software.
She defends her job through tenant **knowledge**, like who can't do mornings.

steps.text: Keep booking tenant repairs by phone with the paper diary
Attend the union branch meeting on new office software rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses are using it as an excuse to cut jobs, because that's what it would be. At Riverside Homes they'd stop replacing people when they leave. I'd share every post about it and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the obvious one to go. I'm junior, I'm slower than Denise (her senior colleague), and I refuse to touch the AI stuff. If they need two admins instead of three, I can do the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly active in the union, not just paying dues. I'd push for a deal that nobody gets sacked because of software, only moved. I'd also look at the council jobs board, because there are lots of office jobs round here, though I know they'd all be changing the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed, and a bit sick in the stomach. I don't like that I'd have to change to keep a job I already do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your manager if she asked you to learn the AI system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll learn it if it's in my hours and there's proper training, not a link to a video. Then I'd probably drag my feet. I know that's not a great plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and plenty of jobs nearby. Why does this one bother you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the other jobs would be changing too, so moving doesn't fix anything. And I chose this one because it's a union place with good pay. I'd lose that and start again at the bottom somewhere worse.

say: Bosses would use AI as an **excuse** to stop replacing staff.
Office workers need **protection** written into union agreements, not promises.
think: As the slowest junior who avoids AI, I'm the **obvious one** to go.
Changing jobs won't help much, because **every office** would be changing the same way.
do: Become an **active** union member and push for no sackings over software.
Ask for **paid training** in work hours before touching the new system.
Check the **council jobs board** for steady office jobs.
feel: **Annoyed** at being made to change, and a bit **sick** about being first out.
S1.quote: I'm junior, I'm slower than Denise (her senior colleague), and I refuse to touch the AI stuff.
fieldNote: She openly admits she'd **drag her feet** even with training.
Her answer to change is **collective**: a union deal rather than personal reinvention.
Plenty of local jobs give little comfort because she expects **all offices** to shift.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-sackings-over-software deal
Check the council jobs board for steady office roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, today, not after it happens. Pay people, slow it down, tax the companies making the money. Online I'd be one of the loud ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job at Riverside Homes (the housing association where she works) is gone, full stop. It's all screen and paper, so there's nothing to hold on to. My savings would carry me maybe a year, and Tomas's bus job only has until the robots, which is three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and every march I could find. I'd stop spending on holidays straight away and keep the eleven months as twelve or thirteen. Then I'd probably look at care work, because helping old people get washed and dressed is hands-on and nobody's AI does that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. And angry that nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can keep the flat, I think. We'd add up his pay without mine and see it just about covers the rent. Then we'd both go quiet, because his buses are only three years behind my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI. Would two years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that's stubborn. Learning AI would just be learning the thing that replaces me. I'd rather spend the time on something a machine can't do yet, like care.

say: Government must **step in now**: support workers and **tax** the companies profiting.
Nobody voted for this, and **ordinary people** weren't asked.
think: My **screen-and-paper** job at Riverside Homes would be gone, full stop.
Tomas's **bus job** only lasts until robots arrive about three years later.
do: Join every **union meeting** and march about AI job losses.
Cut **holidays** at once and stretch savings past a **year**.
Look into **care work**, which is hands-on and harder to automate.
feel: **Scared** about the flat and the future.
S2.quote: My job at Riverside Homes (the housing association where she works) is gone, full stop. It's all screen and paper, so there's nothing to hold on to.
fieldNote: She refuses to learn AI even under pressure; she calls it **learning her replacement**.
Household risk is **stacked**: her desk goes first, her partner's driving three years later.
Her plan B is **care work**, picked because it's hands-on, not because she knows it.

steps.text: Go to every union meeting and march about AI job cuts
Cancel this year's holiday and stretch savings past twelve months
Apply for a care assistant course at the local college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for governments not to plan. Proper retraining money, a law about warning workers, all of it. I'd say it calmer than the two-year one, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be 32 when it hits. Riverside Homes (the housing association where she works) would probably keep me until then, because they're slow with anything new. But I'd be watching the clock the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and stay in the union, but I'd also start a part-time care course in the second year. I'd move a chunk of savings into the account that pays a bit more and not touch it. Around year three, I'd start doing weekend shifts at a care home to see if I can stand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky, more like a dentist appointment I can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work rather than another office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every office goes in the same year, so swapping offices is pointless. Care is hands-on, so it gets the extra three years before robots, and people want a human doing it. I don't love the idea, but I don't hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Denise do, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise (my senior colleague) would learn the new system and try to be the person who runs it. Good luck to her. I just don't think there's a person needed to run it for long.

say: Five years gives governments **no excuse** not to plan.
Workers need a **legal right** to warning and **retraining money**.
think: Riverside Homes is **slow**, so I'd probably keep the job until about **32**.
The deadline would sit in my head like a **clock** ticking the whole time.
do: Keep working and stay active in the **union**.
Start a **part-time care** course in the second year.
Try **weekend shifts** at a care home around year three.
feel: Less panic, more **dread**, like a dentist appointment I **can't cancel**.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd be 32 when it hits. Riverside Homes (the housing association where she works) would probably keep me until then, because they're slow with anything new.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from protest-first to **plan-first**, slowly.
She reasons clearly that **hands-on** care buys three more years than desk work.
Still rejects AI tools; sees the colleague who learns them as **short-lived**.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time care course in the second year
Move savings into the higher-interest account and leave them
Stay active in the union branch at Riverside Homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's do it properly. Shorter weeks, retraining paid for by the firms, housing that doesn't depend on having an office job. I'd probably sound almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd have had ten years to do something about it. That's a career change, not an emergency. I'd still worry, because I know I'm slow to start things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Riverside Homes for a few years and save, maybe aim for eighteen months of money. I'd ask the union to get training into our contract. Then, around 30, I'd train as a nurse, because it's hands-on, it's respected and it pays more than care work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Like there's room to breathe, though I know I'd waste the first two years pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me saying next year, next year. Keeping the paper diary, going to the same café at lunch, not opening the nursing college email. That's honestly how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone I trust doing it first, or the union setting it up so I just turn up. If the nursing course was in work hours I'd go. If it was up to me to sort out alone, I'd put it off.

say: Ten years is enough to do this **properly**, with **shorter weeks** and paid retraining.
Housing shouldn't depend on having an **office job**.
think: At 37 this is a **career change**, not an emergency.
I'm **slow to start**, so I'd probably lose the first two years.
do: Stay at Riverside Homes and build savings to **eighteen months**.
Ask the union to put **training** into the contract.
feel: Some **guilt** that I'd put off starting.
S4.quote: If the nursing course was in work hours I'd go. If it was up to me to sort out alone, I'd put it off.
fieldNote: She is honest about **procrastination**: "next year, next year".
Her best lever is **structure** from the union, not her own drive.
Strong savings and a decade make her **job loss** feel like a planned exit.

steps.text: Build savings up to eighteen months of rent and bills
Ask the union to add paid training to the contract
Apply to train as a nurse around age 30

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, easily. My job goes and Tomas's goes three years later, and I'd have no time to become anything else. What would help is the government actually paying people while they retrain, and the union having a say before the software arrives, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people like me would use the tools if we had a say in them. I might, honestly, if it wasn't being done to me.

headlineQuote: Learning AI would just be learning the thing that replaces me. I'd rather spend the time on something a machine can't do yet, like care.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** junior administrator at Riverside Homes, a housing association, with a strong cushion from her gran.
She refuses **AI tools** and runs her day from a paper diary, partly out of pride.
Her answer to every scenario is **collective**: union deals, government support, taxing the firms that profit.
With two years she's alarmed; with ten she plans a slow move into **nursing**.
She admits she **procrastinates** and needs structure handed to her to change.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because her desk job and her partner's **bus job** would both go close together.
whatWouldHelp: A union **say** before new software arrives, with training in work hours.
